title: Cyrus's Decree: The Exiles May Go Home
summary: In his first year as ruler of Babylon, the Persian king Cyrus issues a proclamation allowing the Jewish exiles to return to Jerusalem and rebuild the house of the LORD. God stirs the hearts of family heads, priests, and Levites to go, and their neighbors send them off with gifts. Cyrus hands over the temple vessels Nebuchadnezzar had taken, and Sheshbazzar brings them to Jerusalem.
story: The last chapters of Kings and Chronicles left Judah in ruins: Jerusalem burned, the temple destroyed, the king and much of the people carried off to Babylon. That was about 587 or 586 BC. Now, some fifty years later, the story starts moving again. The opening words of Ezra repeat the closing words of 2 Chronicles (36:22-23), so the two books join like links in a chain: the story of Israel's kings ends in exile, and the story of the return begins with a foreign king. The chapter reads like a new exodus. As Israel once left Egypt carrying silver and gold from their neighbors, the exiles now leave Babylon loaded with gifts, and the stolen vessels of God's house come home with them. What follows in Ezra is the long, slow work of rebuilding, but it begins here, with God keeping his word.
historical:
Cyrus II, founder of the Persian Empire, captured Babylon in October 539 BC, and the first year of Cyrus in Ezra 1:1 means his first year as king over Babylon, 539/538 BC. Persian royal policy often allowed peoples deported by earlier empires to return home and restore their temples. The Cyrus Cylinder, a clay cylinder discovered at Babylon in 1879 and now in the British Museum, describes Cyrus returning the images of gods to their sanctuaries and gathering their peoples back to their dwellings. The Jews are not named on it, and it concerns cities in Mesopotamia, but it shows the kind of decree Ezra describes. A second, more formal version of Cyrus's order, written in Aramaic as an archive memorandum, appears in Ezra 6:3-5.

The decree says it fulfills the word of the LORD spoken through Jeremiah, who had prophesied that Babylon's rule would last seventy years and that God would then bring his people back (Jeremiah 25:11-12; 29:10). Isaiah had even named Cyrus as the LORD's shepherd who would say of Jerusalem that it should be rebuilt (Isaiah 44:28; 45:1). Sheshbazzar, called the prince of Judah in verse 8 and governor in 5:14, is a figure of some mystery. Some identify him with Zerubbabel, who leads the returnees in chapters 2 to 5; others connect him with Shenazzar, a son of King Jehoiachin (1 Chronicles 3:18); others see him as a Jewish official appointed by Persia who led the first group before Zerubbabel took over.
cultural:
Ancient conquerors carried off the images and sacred objects of defeated peoples and placed them in their own temples, a public sign that their gods had won. Israel had no image of its God, so Nebuchadnezzar took the temple's vessels instead, as 2 Kings 25:13-17 records, and set them in the temple of his gods (verse 7). Returning them was more than a gift of property. It reversed the humiliation, and it signaled that the house of Israel's God would stand again.

The decree describes the LORD as the God of heaven and as the God who is in Jerusalem. The title God of heaven was used in the Persian period for the supreme deity and appears often in Ezra and Nehemiah. Persian kings were accustomed to honor the gods of their subject peoples, and it would be natural for Cyrus's scribes to phrase the decree in terms the Jews themselves would use. The request that neighbors assist the returnees with silver, gold, goods, and livestock fits ancient custom as well; a community sending members on a long trip, especially to a sacred task, supported them.
literary: The chapter has three parts: the decree itself, quoted in Hebrew (verses 2-4); the response of the people, stirred by God and helped by their neighbors (verses 5-6); and the return of the vessels with an exact inventory (verses 7-11). The key verb is stir: the LORD stirs the spirit of Cyrus (verse 1), and he stirs the spirits of those who go up (verse 5). Pagan king and faithful Jew alike move because God moves them. The inventory in verses 9-11 is typical of Ezra, a book that loves lists and exact accounting. The individual figures add up to 2,499, while verse 11 gives a total of 5,400; the Greek book 1 Esdras has different numbers again. The gap probably reflects a problem in copying numbers, which were easily confused in ancient manuscripts, or a total that includes items not itemized.

outline.t: The LORD stirs Cyrus, and the king proclaims the return
The people rise to go, and their neighbors help them
The temple vessels are returned and counted

doctrines.note: God works through a foreign emperor's policy to bring his people home, stirring the spirit of Cyrus without Cyrus becoming a worshiper of the LORD. The chapter teaches that the rise and decisions of empires are under God's hand.
The return happens to fulfill the word of the LORD spoken through Jeremiah. God's word, spoken decades earlier during the disaster, proves reliable, and the book is built on that confidence.

Exile did not end God's commitment to his people. By bringing them back to the land and to the place of his house, he shows that his covenant with Israel survived their unfaithfulness and its punishment.

words.note: Ur, to rouse or stir up, as one wakes a sleeper. The LORD stirs the spirit of Cyrus in verse 1, and in verse 5 everyone whose spirit God had stirred prepares to go. The same verb is used in Isaiah 45:13 of God raising up Cyrus. It frames the whole return as something God set in motion, both in the palace and in ordinary households.

Nasi, a leader or prince, literally one lifted up. In the books of Moses it names tribal chiefs, and Ezekiel uses it for the future ruler of the restored people. Calling Sheshbazzar the prince of Judah gives him honor without the title king, which suits a community under Persian rule.

Golah, the exile or the body of exiles. It becomes a name for the returned community in Ezra (the sons of the golah). The people who return define themselves by the experience of exile and by God bringing them back from it.

christ: The chapter shows God keeping a promise to bring his people home, and the New Testament tells the story of Jesus as the fulfillment of that same hope on a deeper level. Isaiah had called Cyrus the LORD's anointed (Isaiah 45:1), a title that shows God can use even a pagan king for his purposes, but Cyrus is a temporary instrument. The exiles return under his decree and yet remain subjects of Persia, with no son of David on the throne. The prophets of this period keep looking for a greater return and a greater king. The Gospels present Jesus as the anointed one in the full sense, the Son of David who gathers the scattered, and speak of his coming as God visiting and redeeming his people (Luke 1:68). The link is one of pattern and promise: Ezra 1 is a real homecoming that points to one still to come.

hard.q: Why would a pagan Persian king speak of the LORD as the God who appointed him to build a temple in Jerusalem?
hard.a:
Some readers find it unlikely that Cyrus would say that the LORD, the God of heaven, had given him all the kingdoms of the earth. The Cyrus Cylinder shows a similar pattern in Babylon, where Cyrus credits the Babylonian god Marduk with choosing him and calling him to rule. Persian kings routinely honored the gods of their subjects, and official decrees for a particular people were often drafted with the help of members of that people, in their own religious language. So the wording in Ezra 1 does not mean that Cyrus converted. It means that he was willing to present himself as the chosen servant of Judah's God, as he presented himself as the chosen servant of other gods elsewhere.

Some scholars think Ezra's Hebrew version of the decree has been shaped by the Jewish writer, since the Aramaic memorandum in 6:3-5 is plainer. Others argue that both are authentic forms of one decree, one a public proclamation and the other an archive record. Either way, the book's theological point stands: it is the LORD who stirred Cyrus, whatever Cyrus thought he was doing.

questions: God stirred the spirit of a foreign king and of ordinary families alike. Where have you seen good things begin through people who did not know God was using them?
The exiles went home to a ruined city because they believed God's promise. What makes it hard to act on a promise when the circumstances still look bleak?
The vessels taken as trophies came back to their proper place. What would it look like for something taken or misused in your life to be returned to its proper use?
